January, 1993     Page  Reply

 How to write to us...02     -

 Ian Kennedy..........03    07

 Dave Marriott........10    13

 Calvin Allett........15    23

 Alan Cox.............27    35

 G. Robson............41    43

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: Ian Kennedy, BOTSWANA

Dear OUTLET,

         Re: OUTWRITE! v.2
My first reaction to OUTWRITE!
v.2 is "FANTASTISCH". Having
read that it would accept T2
files, I started by trying to
LOAD a DISCIPLE T2 file straight
from Disciple Disc in SAM and,
magic! - it went straight in! I
then SAVEd a MICRODRIVE T2 file
to Disciple and that went
straight in. Then I LOADed T2 on
Microdrive, LOADed an MD file,
switched to Disciple and SAVEd
it and it worked again (some-
thing I never knew). I did the
same with a converted T3 to T2
file (from "OUTLET").


With Dave Tonks TAS t3-t2
CONVERTER (SAM Supplement Issue
No. 24) I can do the same with
my Disciple T3 files. The
implications are tremendous. Not
only are all my T2 and converted
T3 MD files now usable on the
SAM but I don't even need to
SAVE them to SAM disc until I
want to. Also, by merging as
many MD T2 files in TASWORD as
possible, SAVing to Disciple,
LOADing into OUTWRITE2 and block
marking them, I can SAVE them
all separately again with their
original names, saving lots of
time.

This letter will indicate that I
am long in the tooth but those
old files contain the work of


long hours of effort and many
are irreplaceable. (The MDs and
even the Disciple must seize up
some day).

It would bore you to describe
all the other things I like but
it seems to be one of the few
WPs where you can roam with the
cursor anywhere beyond the text
without some dreaded "end of
file" restriction.

Those of you who have battled
with the maddening tab-fixed
text of famous, unnamed best
sellers which dart all over the
place when you try to add things
you have forgot- ten, will know
how valuable cursor roaming can
be.


I don't think many people will
buy your Insert mode argument as
long as it needs two keystrokes
instead of one. Even the new
'SECRETARY' has a "proper"
Insert mode. I'm afraid it's
back to the drawing board for
you.

I have one gripe. How do you
stop the cursor going to the end
of the text from reformat? If
you are editing, you want the
cursor to stay where it is!

Cheers,

          Ian Kennedy

Brian Cavers to Ian Kennedy

Thanks Ian.I agree,I also prefer
the "free-roaming" cursor to the
type that restricts movement yet
some would say it is not"proper"
to use this method!! In the same
way, you are TOTALLY, COMPLETELY
and UTTERLY WRONG to claim that
the OUTWRITE insert mode is not
a "proper" one. I don't care if
ten thousand people misuse the
word"proper",you cannot convince
me that it is appropriate. There
are plenty of other negative
adjectives which I you may feel
apply: "inferior","inefficient",
"less-friendly", "slower" and so
on and on and on but my gripe is
against this word "proper". The
OUWRITE insert mode IS a"proper"
one.

Anyone who thinks it is NOT a
"proper"insert mode on the basis
that many commercial systems use
a different method as standard
must also accept that the SAM
and the Spectrum are not"proper"
computers -they both differ from
the standard PC enormously.

If someone invents a new type of
insert mode using voice control
or even thought control it will
not invalidate existing methods.
Was the BETAMAX video system not
a "proper" video recorder just
because VHS became the standard?
Please, please, please, use a
different adjective. I have no
objection to logical criticism
but I will not this nonsensical
use of the word "proper".

By contrast,your complaint about
the cursor moving to the end of
a paragraph after reforming is
at least put forward sensibly as
a point of view even though I do
not agree! So long as you don't
start saying it is "incorrect"
or not "proper" or "faulty"!Now,
when I write a paragraph, return
to edit and reform it, why would
I want to stay on the line at
which I started to reform? What
do YOU want to do there? If you
have just reformed the paragraph
then it's complete. If you want
to stay in the middle it implies
you are going to do some more
editing at that point so why
reform it? I don't follow that
at all.One usually reforms AFTER
editing and then continue typing
below.                  - Brian

From: Dave Marriott, NOTTINGHAM




Dear Ron and Brian,

I don't think "gobsmacked"
adequately describes how I felt
when reading your editorial in
Issue 64. I knew the financial
situation was pressing, of
course, but to have to close
through lack of contributions
seems crazy. It galls me to
think that those neanderthals
with Spectrums (no offence, I
was one once!)can produce enough
to keep a magazine going, but
those of us with superior
machines can't.

I initially thought that the
editorial was a last, desperate
"Get your fingers out!" message
to SAM programmers, but reading
on, you didn't give cause for
much hope. Is it as definite as
that? If it stirred enough SAM
programmers into sending in an
adequate volume of stuff, would
there be any chance of a stay of
execution, or even a reprieve? I
realise that the stark equation
of less programmers and more
disczines compared to the Spec-
trum is always going to be
against us but is there no other
way out?

I'm sure there are plenty of
people who enjoy programming the
SAM but can't always think of

something to write; would there
be any mileage in a system where
you or subscribers suggest
programs they'd like to see, and
others volunteer to write them?

I sincerely hope the SAM version
of OUTLET can continue in some
way,if not indefinitely,then for
as long as possible. True, there
are quite a few other SAM disc-
zines, but with no disrespect to
them, OUTLET is the best. If it
does come to the crunch, though,
thanks for all the enjoyment
you've given us over the past
few years, and good luck with
the remaining Spectrum version.
We'll miss you.

             Dave Marriott

Brian Cavers to Dave Marriott

Right from Issue 1,our policy is
never to harangue or pester our
readers for more contributions.
We have never felt it to be the
responsibility of our readers to
support OUTLET but that it is
OUR responsibility to support
our readers. Despite our best
efforts we have failed.

In the last two months, when we
saw the falling contributions,we
could have taken desperate steps
to muddle through for a few more
months but because the cash flow
was already below crisis point,
the writing was clearly on the
wall and there seemed no purpose
in postponing the inevitable.

Even if we now became flooded
with contributions it would make
little difference in the end as
we need more sales and cannot
continue losing money each month
indefinitely with no reasonable
hope of a miraculous upturn in a
small, closed market.

Morale had been low here for
some time because of the extreme
financial difficulties so there
was little spirit left for a
fight when we saw contributions
dwindling too!

Never mind! It was fun while it
lasted!
                        - Brian

From:  C. Allett, NORTHUMBERLAND

Dear Ron and Brian,

First, let me say how sorry I am
that you are being forced to
stop producing OUTLET for the
SAM. I, for one, will greatly
miss it.

In my last letter (Issue 64) I
said I didn't agree with what
Colin MacDonald had said about
people contributing to existing
mags, I didn't actually mean
that I thought there weren't too
many mags on the SAM, what I did
mean though is that it isn't
necessarily a bad thing. The
reason I think this is because
if there are a lot of mags. then


there is going to be more soft-
ware. If, say, one mag has all
the usual 'good' contributors
then people that aren't quite so
talented will not be able to get
their programs in that mag, but
they may be able to get a newer
magazine,that needs programs, to
use them. In this way more
software gets seen and on the
SAM, that's good.

The bad points are that people
get spoilt for choice and may
not buy a certain mag. because
they just never get round to it
or simply cannot afford it and
also great mags like OUTLET also
suffer which is a shame because
of all the mags I've seen,OUTLET
seems to be about the only
serious one.

I hope you'll have enough soft-
ware to be able to release Issue
66. I've included some software
that I did ages ago; it's not
great as I was just starting to
learn to program when I did them
but I hope it helps.

Are you still making back issues
of both SAM and Spectrum 128K
tape versions available because
I may wish to order some. If so,
how much are they?

Thanks for the help with the
POINT command, the XOS, XRG etc.
variables were correct so it's
not that so I think you must be
right about the paging problems.
I'll try what you said when I've
got the time.


Regarding the sector errors, the
problem wasn't because of leav-
ing disks in when resetting be-
cause I've only ever done that
once - (by mistake, and it did
cause a sector error).


Since thinking about it I think
I may know why it happened. I
always have a 'Working Disk'
which I use when programming.
Whenever I program something, I
then SAVE it. Then, as I improve
the program etc.,I keep reSAVing
the latest version over the old
one and also over the backup
copy; by doing this I normally
SAVE programs onto the disk at
least 5 or 6 times a day.



Also, if I decide a program is
totally crap then I erase it, so
the disk gets used lots. When
it's nearly full I start using a
new disk. I think all this
SAVing, reSAVing and ERASing
could be causing sector errors.
Is this possible?

Just about everybody seems to be
wanting upgrades for their SAMs,
DMA, hardware scrolling, a
blitter etc, Colin MacDonald
even got 'told off' for being
negative but I think he's right.

What's the point of building new
SAMs with one or more of these
or bringing them out for people
to maybe fit themselves. There
is very little software being


released for the SAM now and if
people did have this extra hard-
ware then there would probably
be no software made to support
it. There aren't enough normal
SAMs around to justify commerc-
ial games, let alone enhanced
ones.


Do they really think that if a
new SAM was designed and produc-
ed with hardware scrolling and
DMA then suddenly flocks of peo-
ple would by it? If they do then
they're living in a dream world.
People are even buying consoles
instead of the Amiga because
they consider the Amiga isn't
good enough or is dated - and
that has lots of custom chips.


The 32 bit Amiga A1200 has just
been released at a price of `400
and that has a 14Mhz 32-bit
processor, 16,777,216 colours,
256 colours on screen, better
graphics potential than the old
ones and much more. How can a
`200 eight-bit computer expect
to compete?

Having said all that, custom
chips can do a lot even for an 8
bit. The Super Nintendo has only
an 8-bit processor but because
of its two super graphics chips,
it performs brilliantly.

Extra chips wouldn't do the SAM
any good because people either
want 32-bit computers like the
Archimedes/Falcon and Amiga


A1200 or they want those annoy-
ing console thingies that I hate
like the Megadrive or SNES. I'm
sorry if this upsets anybody but
as I see it, that's the way
things are. I'm even saving for
the A1200 myself but I'll still
use my SAM.

One last thing, I wonder what
type of mentality all these con-
sole owners must have to pay an
average of `50 for a game. If
they are that stupid then they
should be shot. The main thing I
use my SAM for is programming
and I find that just as enjoy-
able as playing games and at
least it's constructive.

All the best for the future,
                 - Calvin Allett

Brian Cavers to Calvin Allett

Yes, all back issues are still
available and are `3.50 for any
version.

Heavy use of a disc should not
cause sector errors. It is more
likely the disc was already bad
in higher sector numbers but to
begin with you may only be using
the lower sectors. As more and
more disc space is used (either
by adding more files or expand-
ing a developing program) then
eventually a SAVE may reach the
bad sectors. The verify built in
to the FORMAT is not reliable. A
more reliable method is to use a
FORMAT and then load in all the
sectors one by one using...

10 FOR T=0 TO 207
20 IF T=80 THEN LET T=128
30 FOR S=1 TO 10
40 READ AT 1,T,S,55555
50 NEXT S
60 NEXT T

If all the sectors load then you
know the disc is O.K. MASTERDOS
is faster because you can load
more than one sector at a time
or you could just copy the disc
to a spare using FORMAT d1 to d2
if you have two drives. Don't
use BACK UP for this purpose as
it doesn't waste time copying
empty sectors (which may be the
very bad ones you are trying to
detect). All this is tedious but
it's worth considering if only
for the odd disc with important
files.

I agree,no matter what bells and
whistles might be added to the
SAM's hardware, it will never be
a huge seller now.If it had been
launched under licence to
Amstrad instead of the Plus 3 as
the next official Spectrum with
48K and 128K Spectrum ROMs built
in (as well as the new SAM ROM
of course), it would have been a
sensational success with every
dealer begging to stock it! Any
later hardware additions would
indeed have then built on that
success.

Still, that's all pie in the sky
because the SAM could probably
not have been created at that
earlier date any more than the
Amiga could have been launched
before the first Spectrum!

As for console owners, I don't
think they're necessarily stupid
but I'm just astonished they can
afford these games. I like to
watch BAD INFLUENCE on ITV which
is much better than GAMESMASTER
on Channel 4. In their review
section they have little 10-year
old kids saying things like...
"I'll definitely get this one -
it's great!" and up above is the
price of say, `44.95!! What sort
of pocket money do kids get
these days! These reviewers talk
as if they get a few new games
every month! They can't copy the
cartridges and surely they can't
keep persuading parents to part
with that sort of money on a
regular basis - not your average
earner at any rate!
                        - Brian

From: Alan D. Cox, ST.CLEARS

Dear Brian,

Here are my brief comments to
various points in Issue 63... I
was surprised at the somewhat
intemperate comments on my view
that OUTLET should try to keep
to the lowest common denominator
of SAM BASIC and DOS: I do not
feel there is anything much to
be added to your sound and
cogent comments on this point.
In my view the SAM community
needs to be very wary of the
pressure from sellers of new
products to BUY!, BUY!, BUY! -
something that is only too
familiar in the PC world, with
its frenetic upgrading fever.


There are very few things that I
cannot do with the 'basic' SAM -
after all, those of us who have
come up via the Spectrum/
Disciple have had to learn to do
without the frills.

When I have exhausted all the
possibilities, and learnt all I
can, about the basic SAM and its
software, then I might think
about upgrades. I estimate that
this might be in about ten years
time!

I am afraid Cliff Jackson has
misread my letter about Spectrum
128k etc. My point, which I
thought was clear, was that I
was quoting Specman who claimed
to have done the conversion,


and I was asking, since I should
also be interested, if anyone
really understood what he had
done.

I am grateful to Ettrick Thomson
for his comments on the Easter
day algorithm. However,I would
point out that the fault is not
with the algorithm, which as far
as I know accurately calculates
what it sets out to do, but in
my careless description of it -
it is the old problem that I was
too close to the problem and
failed to spell out a point that
was obvious to me: ie that the
algorithm calculates the date
for Easter Day from 1583
ACCORDING TO THE NEW STYLE
CALENDAR.


I felt that in the circumstances
I ought to adapt the algorithm
to give Old Style dates, and I
have put a somewhat inelegant
'tweak' of the original on the
disk [in ADD-ENDERS - Ed].

Because of the curious nature of
the calculation of the date of
Easter, it is not merely a
question of taking off the 12
days - in certain years Easter
Day is actually a different day
under the two dating styles, not
just the same day assigned a
different label.

Does anyone know whether there
are copies of full compilers for
the 48k Spectrum still available
(I have got ZIP and BLAST)?

ZIP is very fast but is limited
in what it can do, whereas BLAST
goes only a little faster than
BASIC. W.A.V.E. have one in
their catalogue but they tell me
they cannot supply it.

I've now upgraded to 512K but,
frankly, I rarely need so large
a memory. Is it possible to LOAD
two or more separate BASIC prog-
rams into RAM and then choose to
run any of them on command? In
principle I cannot see why not,
but I fear I'm not clever enough
to work out how to do it. I am
not, of course, asking for all
programs to run at the same time
- this would involve a much
deeper set of arrangements to
'time- share' the CPU, even if
it were possible.

Thinking about your problems
with SAM material,I was reminded
of a comment I made in one of my
letters following my get-to-
gether with Danny Beach, when I
noticed the Spectrum version of
OUTLET appeared to occupy many
less bytes on disk than the SAM
version. If this is true as a
general rule, then would it be
feasible to use spare space on
the Spectrum disks to publish
SAM-related material? Clearly,
we would not get the excellent
presentational aspects of SAM
OUTLET, but for me it would be
very much better than nothing,
which is all that is on offer at
the moment, You could put the
onus on those who offer items to
set up their own presentation.


I know you operate a policy of
open-ness in all you publish,
but I realise there may be a few
'trade secrets', so if you do
not wish to respond to the
following, then so be it.

In OUTLET 53, DEMOPIX you have
as number 2, 'Flying Falls',
which shows a picture of a comp-
lex waterfall with the water
apparently flowing along and
down.Now, this is almost exactly
the effect I want to achieve
with a representation of one of
the famous M.C. Escher pictures
- in this case the one where a
staircase around a square well
seems to continue to go down for
ever, I thought it would be use-
ful to make the point by having


water flowing downwards, and
obviously an adaptation of
'Flying Falls' would do the job.

I have looked at the BASIC
DEMOPIX 19", but I do not see
what is going on, except at the
elementary level that a set of
bytes is being rotated around.
Could you cast some light on
this matter, please? It may well
be that it is tied up with the
screen compression system,
although I think this is in a
separate area of RAM.

        All best wishes

          Alan D. Cox.

Brian Cavers to Alan Cox

My understanding was that the
HISOFT compiler was the best but
I must admit I never had the
opportunity to use it.It used to
be available from MICROSNIPS,
25-29 Grange Road West, Birken-
head, Merseyside, L41 4BY (051
650 0500) for `21.95 (ask for
HISOFT BASIC). I would ring them
first to see if they still stock
it.

I believe HISOFT went on to
produce software for other 16-
bit machines but they may still
be able to supply the Spectrum
compiler if MICROSNIPS cannot.
Does anyone know their current
address?

Ah! Here's another address.Again
it is out of date so ring them
first... LION COMPUTERS, 778
Borough Road, Birkenhead,Mersey-
side, L42 9JG (051 255 o625).
They use to advertise HISOFT
BASIC at `24.95. I would stress
you want it for the Spectrum
else you might get an ST version
or something!

My recollection is that the
compiler dealt with most of the
BASIC commands but using integer
numbers. However, I have an idea
it could be set to deal with
decimal fractions but would be
much slower in that mode of
course. This is only a hazy
memory so don't take my word for
it.

It should be possible to load 2
(and more) BASIC programs into
SAM's memory and select them to
run as needed by setting various
flags.Malcolm Goodman wrote such
a routine for the Spectrum and,
if he says this, may like to
experiment! There is a problem
in that SAM BASIC stores the
actual memory addresses of GOTOs
and procedures etc in the actual
listing - just after the command
words I think.

It probably is not worth it any-
way.If you get MASTERDOS you can
set up a RAMDISK and save and
load programs to memory almost
instantly. On reflection, it is
hardly worth re-inventing the
wheel; I doubt one could improve
on MASTERDOS's method.

No, I have no plans to put "SAM
bits" on to the Disciple disc. I
have enough worries and I doubt
many people would want to spend
`3.50 for a part-disc when there
aren't enough buying the full
disc. In any case,I want to keep
the Disciple disc free for more
expansion.

Most(but not all) of the DEMOPIX
animation is done by rotating
the palette colours. This is
achieved with a special picture
that is drawn with several
copies of the object(s) or area
being moved at various points
along the screen each using a
different palette number in
sequence (e.g., say, numbers 4
to 9).

The actual colour number for all
of these images BUT ONE is set
to a background colour and so is
invisible. Imagine a simple ball
rolling from left to right. Draw
say, six identical balls side by
side, one using INK 4, the next
using INK 5 and so on...

BALL: O    O    O    O    O    O

INK:  4    5    6    7    8    9

Now, if the background is say,0,
palette 4 is say, 68 (green) and
palette 5 to 9 are 0 then the
ball images 5 to 9 will be the
same colour as the background
and so invisible. Only ball 4
will be visible. The palette is
now "rotated" so the next image
becomes green and the first 0...

The palette values are stored
starting with palette 0 at
address 21976 so 4 is at 21980.
If you study the ANIMATE proced-
ure in DEMOPIX you will see how
that is POKEd to rotate the
values. Note also that each
palette value is duplicated 20
addresses higher. This is how
the SAM produces flashing colour
so these must be identical if
you don't want flashing. All the
values are picked up automatic-
ally by the system's interrupt
routines and fed to the colour
register every fiftieth of a
second. The whole thing could be
done using the PALETTE command
but would probably be too slow.
It would be difficult, perhaps
impossible, to adapt an existing
picture to do all this. - Brian

From: G. Robson, WEST YORKS.

Dear Sirs,

I wonder if you can explain
something to me which I came
across recently. I purchased the
"Dizzy Excellent Adventures"
(Spectrum version), LOADed each
game one at a time into my
Spectrum +3, and using 'THE
MESSENGER' transferred them on
to a disc for my SAM Coupe.

Four of the games reLOADed O.K.
from the disc (apart from a few
joystick and key controls being
a bit odd), but one game,
"Spellbound Dizzy", when reLOAD-
ed from the disc appeared to be
running at double speed!


The little egg,although respond-
ing to the joystick controls,
was dashing around the screen at
such a rate it was impossible to
play the game. Also some of the
screens were flashing on and
off. Yet, when LOADed on the
Spectrum +3, the game played at
a normal speed. I have transfer-
red a number of games using 'THE
MESSENGER' before but have never
come across anything like this.
Usually, if a game does not
transfer, and quite a number do
not, you tend to get a locked up
game or nothing at all.

Have you any clue as to what is
happening and is there any cure?

           G. Robson


Brian Cavers to G. Robson

All Spectrum games run slightly
faster on the SAM Coupe because
it uses the Z80B processor which
is more efficient the the Z80A
which is in the Spectrum.However
it does sound excessive if it is
moving at DOUBLE speed! Because
an exact copy of Spectrum memory
are copied into the SAM,the only
difference can be in hardware
normally accessed with IN and
OUT codes. My guess is "DIZZY"
plays 128K music on a 128K Spec-
trum and calls it every fraction
of a second with an IN/OUT code.
The time taken by the 128K music
may be replaced by a delay on a
48K Spectrum to keep the speed
right but on SAM - nothing!

All this is wild guesswork and
it can only be resolved by time-
consuming hacking into the code.
Unless anyone else has solved
this problem then you are very
unlikely to get it to work
properly.

It is also worth trying a method
of emulation other than using a
Messenger. For example, if you
have OUTLET 33 you could try the
games using EMUTILITY.I have got
DIZZY 3 working OK using it (the
one that starts with the troll
and the apple etc.). Programmers
tend to use the same routines in
different games so the other
DIZZY games "should" work. It is
worth a try so long as your tape
deck works alright with your SAM
Coupe.                   - Brian.

From: Ian Kennedy, BOTSWANA

10 FOR T=0 TO 207 20 IF T=80 THEN LET T=128 30 FOR S=1 TO 10 40 READ AT 1,T,S,55555 50 NEXT S 60 NEXT T

Most(but not all) of the DEMOPIX animation is done by rotating the palette colours. This is achieved with a special picture that is drawn with several copies of the object(s) or area being moved at various points along the screen each using a different palette number in sequence (e.g., say, numbers 4 to 9).

The actual colour number for all of these images BUT ONE is set to a background colour and so is invisible. Imagine a simple ball rolling from left to right. Draw say, six identical balls side by side, one using INK 4, the next using INK 5 and so on...

BALL: O    O    O    O    O    O

```text
INK:  4    5    6    7    8    9
```

Now, if the background is say,0, palette 4 is say, 68 (green) and palette 5 to 9 are 0 then the ball images 5 to 9 will be the same colour as the background and so invisible. Only ball 4 will be visible. The palette is now "rotated" so the next image becomes green and the first 0...

The palette values are stored starting with palette 0 at address 21976 so 4 is at 21980. If you study the ANIMATE proced- ure in DEMOPIX you will see how that is POKEd to rotate the values. Note also that each palette value is duplicated 20 addresses higher. This is how the SAM produces flashing colour so these must be identical if you don't want flashing. All the values are picked up automatic- ally by the system's interrupt routines and fed to the colour register every fiftieth of a second. The whole thing could be done using the PALETTE command but would probably be too slow. It would be difficult, perhaps impossible, to adapt an existing picture to do all this. - Brian

Большая часть (хотя и не вся) анимации в DEMOPIX сделана с помощью циклического сдвига (ротации) цветов палитры. Это достигается за счет специальной картинки, на которой несколько копий двигающегося объекта (или области) нарисованы в разных точках экрана, и каждая копия использует свой порядковый номер палитры (например, с 4 по 9).

Фактический цвет для всех этих копий, КРОМЕ ОДНОЙ, устанавливается равным цвету фона и потому невидим. Представьте себе простой мячик, катящийся слева направо. Нарисуйте, скажем, шесть одинаковых мячиков в ряд, один с INK 4, следующий с INK 5 и так далее...

```text
МЯЧ:  O    O    O    O    O    O

INK:  4    5    6    7    8    9
```

Теперь, если фон, допустим, 0, цвет палитры 4 — скажем, 68 (зеленый), а палитры с 5 по 9 равны 0, то мячики с 5 по 9 сольются с фоном и станут невидимыми. Виден будет только мяч под номером 4. Затем палитра «сдвигается», так что зеленым становится следующий объект, а первый получает 0...

Значения палитры хранятся начиная с палитры 0 по адресу 21976, то есть палитра 4 находится по адресу 21980. Если вы изучите процедуру ANIMATE в DEMOPIX, то увидите, как туда делаются POKE для сдвига значений. Заметьте также, что каждое значение палитры дублируется на 20 адресов выше. Именно так SAM реализует мерцание цвета (FLASH), поэтому эти значения должны быть идентичны, если мерцание вам не нужно. Все значения считываются автоматически системными процедурами прерываний и передаются в регистр цвета каждые 1/50 секунды. Всё это можно было бы сделать с помощью команды PALETTE, но это было бы слишком медленно. Адаптировать уже готовую картинку под такой трюк будет трудно, если вообще возможно. — Brian.

Все спектрумовские игры идут на SAM Coupe немного быстрее, поскольку в нем используется процессор Z80B, который работает эффективнее, чем установленный в Спектруме Z80A. Однако ДВОЙНАЯ скорость — это, конечно, перебор! Поскольку в SAM копируется точный слепок памяти Спектрума, единственная разница может крыться в портах ввода-вывода (команды IN и OUT). Моя догадка: DIZZY на 128K Спектруме воспроизводит 128K-музыку, вызывая ее через порт IN/OUT долю секунды за долей секунды. На 48K Спектруме время, уходившее на эту музыку, заменяется искусственной задержкой для поддержания нормальной скорости, а на SAM — ничего подобного нет!

Впрочем, все это лишь догадки, и разобраться тут можно, только потратив кучу времени на взлом кода. Если только кто-то другой уже не решил эту проблему, шансов заставить ее работать как надо очень мало.

Также стоит попробовать другой способ эмуляции, помимо The Messenger. Например, если у вас есть OUTLET 33, вы можете попробовать запустить игры с помощью EMUTILITY. У меня с ее помощью нормально заработал DIZZY 3 (тот, что начинается с тролля, яблока и т.д.). Программисты обычно используют одни и те же подпрограммы в разных играх, так что и другие части DIZZY «должны» работать. Попробовать определенно стоит — главное, чтобы магнитофон нормально работал с вашим SAM Coupe.
